aboutyou.first_line: I've spent my whole career helping schools get better: from the classroom, from inside networks, and as a consultant in over a hundred schools.
aboutyou.script:
I've spent my whole career helping schools get better: from the classroom, from inside networks, and as a consultant in over a hundred schools.

I started as a teacher in DC, then went to Excel Academy in Boston for a turnaround. I ran culture and operations, and we took the school from **270th in the state to number one** and National Charter School of the Year. While I was there I built a tool we needed and turned it into DeansList. I grew it from zero to 275 schools. It's in over a thousand now, though I haven't been affiliated in years.

Excel's success brought a lot of visitors, and some became my first clients. So I started a consulting practice and got to walk into 100 schools, KIPP, Uncommon, Achievement First and a lot of regional operators, and help principals fix problems.

That's how I got to Collegiate Academies in New Orleans. I was brought in to Carver to work with a principal who wasn't sure he could do the job. [beat] Jerel went on to be Louisiana Principal of the Year, and now he runs Collegiate. I moved down and was Chief Culture Officer for five years.

Then we came back to Brooklyn. I was superintendent at Brooklyn Lab for a transitional period, to stabilize, lead and pass off. We led through COVID and took both charters through renewal at the same time, and both were reauthorized. Then two years at the KIPP Foundation, bringing 28 very independent regions into alignment. We built a national high school strategy and handed it back to the regions. Now I build custom AI tools for school leaders, so they can focus on the real work.

whyzeta.first_line: Because what I've done my whole career is **build things other people can run**, and that's this job.
whyzeta.script:
Because what I've done my whole career is **build things other people can run**, and that's this job.

The work is taking initiatives from launch to practices the whole organization uses. I love building systems and structures that people buy into **on merit, not out of obligation**.

This seat is close to schools and close to network decision makers. That's a great way to get to know the org, the schools and the people. And I've got a lot of high school experience in operations, culture and academics, so the high school question really excites me.

I also like how you work. Excellence with exploration. Best idea wins. Strong opinions, loosely held. [beat] Let's debate the heck out of things, and attack ideas without attacking people.

carver.first_line: I was brought in to Carver as a consultant with one question: **do we keep this leader?**
carver.script:
I was brought in to Carver as a consultant with one question: **do we keep this leader?**

Jerel Bryant was the founding principal, in year three, and a really compelling, charismatic leader. But the school was struggling with academics, student culture and community relations. Teachers were frustrated and acting like negative controllers. Kids were pushing back, skipping class and opting out of learning.

What I saw was a **high-potential leader getting a lot of criticism and very little help**. So I worked shoulder to shoulder with him, with high doses of real-time feedback. Mostly affirming, so he'd stop second-guessing himself. [beat] I named the relationship that needed to be reset, and we focused people on results and impact, not blame.

Jerel was great with kids, so we **put that on stage**. We spent hours on the floor coaching and modeling, showing teachers what it looks like to invest, direct and redirect scholars. It worked. Students started to feel like school was safe, predictable and purposeful.

[land] In our fourth year together, Jerel was Louisiana Principal of the Year, and today he's CEO of Collegiate Academies. [STOP]
carver.landing: In our fourth year together, Jerel was Louisiana Principal of the Year, and today he's CEO of Collegiate Academies.

managed.first_line: Yes to both: I managed three principals as superintendent at Brooklyn Lab, and I was interim high school principal for half a year.
managed.script:
Yes to both: I managed three principals as superintendent at Brooklyn Lab, and I was interim high school principal for half a year.

At Brooklyn Lab I was there for a transitional period, to stabilize, lead and pass off. I led the three principals and the C-level team. I was responsible for **academic results directly through the principals**, and I led the summer onboarding and all the learning and development.

Two of my three schools didn't see their superintendent in the building for a semester. They got their principal and my phone. [beat] What they needed was **a decision maker who answered fast**, not a superintendent who visited. I made that trade at the semester line, not in June.

While I was superintendent, I also made the call to remove a principal and take the school over myself as interim, because it needed to be done.

And before that, at Collegiate, I was brought in to assess and coach principals. [land] At Carver, that principal was Jerel, who went on to be Louisiana Principal of the Year. [STOP]
managed.landing: At Carver, that principal was Jerel, who went on to be Louisiana Principal of the Year.

ownership.first_line: Once a high school is functional, two corners make all the difference: **academic identity** and **real student ownership**.
ownership.script:
Once a high school is functional, two corners make all the difference: **academic identity** and **real student ownership**.

At Excel we got to functional. Not perfect, but working and academically focused. Then we turned those two corners.

First, identity. What teachers did bell to bell built a sense that it's cool to be smart and cool to work hard. Middle school might run on incentives and team. High school gets more individual and more rigorous. It's not fun because it's fun. It's fun because it's challenging.

Second, ownership that isn't thin and surfacey. Student groups that help run the school during the day. An honor council that looks into honor code violations and makes recommendations, within limits. An events committee that plans the dance, hypes it, attaches a service commitment and makes the announcements. [beat] At 150 kids a grade, you can get **more than a third of students** in a meaningful group. That's how a kid gets to "it's my school."

[slow] Adults say a whole lot less, and students say a whole lot more. [land] Our orientation leaders, sophomores and juniors, ran 50% of freshman orientation. [STOP]
